paragraphs.heading: Pathways through the sea
paragraphs.text: Chemical substances and elements move through the sea along pathways. The pathways they follow through the salt water of seas and oceans, and through the brackish water of coastal estuaries, are called marine biogeochemical cycles. There are cycles for elements such as carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur, and for the molecules water and silica.

paragraphs.heading: Why the long name
paragraphs.text: Three kinds of force drive these cycles. One is metabolism inside living things, one is geological processes involving the Earth’s mantle, and one is chemical reactions among the substances themselves. That is why they are called biogeochemical cycles. These forces can break substances down and recombine them, but they cannot create or destroy the chemical elements. A little is lost to outer space and a little gained from it. Otherwise an element is either recycled or stored somewhere on or inside the planet.

paragraphs.heading: What living things use
paragraphs.text: Six elements are the ones most commonly found in organic molecules. They are carbon, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur. Carbon is in every organic molecule. Nitrogen is an important part of nucleic acids and proteins. Phosphorus goes into nucleic acids and into the phospholipids that make up biological membranes, and proteins depend on sulfur for their three-dimensional shape. Marine organisms, and marine microorganisms in particular, are crucial to keeping many of the cycles working.

paragraphs.heading: Water carries everything
paragraphs.text: Water is the medium of the oceans, and it carries every substance and element involved in these cycles. Water in nature almost always has other substances dissolved in it, which is why it has been called the “universal solvent”. Because liquid water flows, ocean waters travel in currents around the world. Water also changes phase easily. It can rise into the atmosphere as vapour or freeze into an iceberg, and later precipitate or melt into liquid again.

paragraphs.heading: From the land to the sea
paragraphs.text: Substances can also be brought into the marine environment or carried out of it. These exchanges happen with the atmosphere above, with the ocean floor below, and as runoff from the land. Moving water leaches phosphorus and sulfur into rivers, and rivers can flow on into the oceans. Runoff accounts for almost all of the eroded sediment and phosphorus that travels from land to waterbodies. Runoff and groundwater flow both play significant roles in carrying nitrogen the same way.

paragraphs.heading: Fertilizer downstream
paragraphs.text: Fertilizer travels by the same routes. Phosphorus spread in excess on farm fields as fertilizer, then carried overland and down rivers, is the main cause of a problem in lakes called cultural eutrophication. At the outlet of the Mississippi River there is a dead zone. It exists because fertilizer nitrates are washed off farm fields and funnelled by the river system into the Gulf of Mexico.

paragraphs.heading: Where the salt comes from
paragraphs.text: The salt in the ocean comes mainly from the weathering of rocks and from dissolved salts carried off the land, with smaller contributions from hydrothermal vents in the seafloor. Evaporation and the forming of sea ice raise salinity further. Fresh water from rivers, rain and snow, and melting ice continually push it back down. Chloride and sodium are the two most prevalent ions in seawater. Between them they account for around 85 per cent of the ocean’s dissolved ions.
